evidence.title: Unverified Vendor Claims and Preventable Harms: A Mixed-Methods Longitudinal Independent Audit of Health AI System Performance in Nigeria
evidence.outcome: gap between vendor claims and real-world accuracy
evidence.effect: Real-world accuracy averaged 67.3%, yielding a mean performance gap of 24.2 percentage points lower than vendor-reported accuracy of 91.5%.
evidence.quote: Vendor-reported accuracy averaged 91.5%, while independently measured real-world accuracy averaged 67.3%, yielding a mean performance gap of 24.2 percentage points (95% CI: 21.5 to 26.9; p<0.001) across systems.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether requiring and assessing vendor validation evidence before purchase, or reassessing it across adoption stages, improves AI performance or patient outcomes. One descriptive study from rural Nigeria found real-world accuracy 24.2 percentage points below vendor-reported accuracy, which shows the hazard exists but does not show that pre-purchase review closes the gap.

perspectives.view: Eight sources endorse the practice, three as a requirement and five as advice, but all are guidance, frameworks, or commentary. No trial, cohort, or before-after study compares procurement with and without validation review. The single supplied study documents the hazard only, so certainty about the practice's effect cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

In one real deployment covering 52,000 patients, real-world accuracy averaged 67.3% against a vendor-reported 91.5%. A gap of this size suggests that tools accepted on vendor figures alone may misclassify many more patients than buyers expect. Whether local verification before purchase would have caught this gap remains untested.

The only study drew on rural patients in Nigeria and found a 24.2-point accuracy shortfall. This finding may indicate that vendor figures transfer poorly to populations unlike the development data. The study did not examine Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups in U.S. settings, and no study tested whether subgroup evidence at procurement protects them.

Patients generally cannot see what accuracy evidence a health system reviewed before buying a tool. The Nigerian study suggests that a vendor's stated accuracy may overstate real performance by roughly a quarter. No study shows how pre-purchase review affects patient trust or harm, so the benefit to patients is assumed rather than measured.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare health systems or tool acquisitions that apply structured vendor-evidence review, including subgroup and calibration data and staged reassessment, with those that do not. Outcomes should include the size of the gap between claimed and local performance, the rate of tools rejected or withdrawn, patient harm events, and the staff time and cost the review requires.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The single hazard study included rural patients in Nigeria, which suggests that vendor accuracy claims may fall short in low-resource settings, but it did not include U.S. Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on whether pre-purchase validation review detects performance gaps for their patients.
